newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Safety measures hamper Mississippi commerce.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Safety measures hamper Mississippi commerce.

text.p: Commerce on the Mississippi is being severely disrupted as the river faces its heaviest spring run-off in more than 60 years, according to commercial vessel operators.
In a move likely to further hamper traffic, the Coast Guard on Friday added more safety restrictions because of surging floodwaters and a dangerously fast current.

"We have never as an inudustry had to resort to this level of safety on the Mississippi...(and) it is significantly slowing things down," said Ken Wells, southern area vice president of the American Waterways Operators, a Washington-based trade association representing cargo carriers.
"But there is enough concern for safety that nobody has been complaining," Wells added.

The Coast Guard ruled Friday that tank vessels or tank ships with 1,600 gross tons or more carryng certain petroleum products or chemicals, as well as deep-draft chemical tank ships, must travel in daylight hours only between mile 88 (New Orleans) and mile 233 (Baton Rouge) of the river.

A number of restrictions already in place, such as a sharp cut in tugboat loads, has cut "by a third to half" the commercial river traffic, said Wells, who added that backed-up traffic at the industrial canal lock at New Orleans and elsewhere also is adding to delays.

"The last time (the river) got this high was 1983 (and) the current is more difficult to deal with," said John Cascio, general manager of Moran Gulf Shipping Agencies in New Orleans, whose company handles 18 ships.
"But it would be irresponsible to shut down the river. There's so much commerce, a total shutdown would cripple a lot of people," Cascio said.

Last Tuesday, Louisiana governor Murphy J. Foster warned large industry along the river that he might press the Coast Guard for a total shutdown of the river if he thought the population were at risk.

That was followed Wednesday by the evacuation of five government buildings and schools near the governor's office in Baton Rouge after some people complained of dizziness and blurred vision. The evacuation was linked to a barge which capsized on March 17 after its tow hit the U.S. 190 bridge in Baton Rouge, spilling a liquid hydrocarbon containing toxic benzene.

The traffic restrictions are a compromise which followed days of discussions between Coast Guard officials and the Louisiana governor, and lobbying by large industry, especially chemical and petro-chemical concerns.
"Nobody can afford to have one of these accidents when you look at what's going on in Baton Rouge," said Wells.
He said the disruptions are hitting chemicals and petrochemicals plants most, while the effect on dry cargo and agricultural commodities will take longer to filter through.
"Chemicals and petrochemicals, that is where you are going to see the first critical problems. We are moving them with an unprecedented level of care," said Wells.

The Mississippi is one of the world's busiest waterways, with around half-a-million tons of cargo traffic a year, according to U.S. Army Corps of Engineers data. Around a quarter of that consists of oil and oil products and chemicals, the figures show.
--((Tony McAuley/Ransdell Pierson, New York Energy Desk, +1 212 859 1620))
